I'll analyze each molecule based on my knowledge of molecular geometry and dipole moments:

A. C2F4 (Tetrafluoroethylene): This molecule has a C=C double bond with two F atoms attached to each carbon. The structure is planar and has a symmetrical distribution of the highly electronegative fluorine atoms. Due to this symmetry, the individual C-F bond dipoles cancel out, resulting in a net dipole moment of zero.

B. CF4 (Carbon tetrafluoride): This molecule has a tetrahedral geometry with the carbon atom at the center and four fluorine atoms at the corners of the tetrahedron. The tetrahedral structure is perfectly symmetrical, and although each C-F bond is polar, the vector sum of all bond dipoles is zero due to the symmetrical arrangement.

C. SF4 (Sulfur tetrafluoride): This molecule has a see-saw (or disphenoidal) geometry with the sulfur atom at the center. It has four fluorine atoms and one lone pair of electrons. The lone pair occupies one equatorial position in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. This creates an asymmetrical distribution of electron density, resulting in a non-zero dipole moment.

D. SF6 (Sulfur hexafluoride): This molecule has an octahedral geometry with the sulfur atom at the center and six fluorine atoms arranged symmetrically around it. Due to this perfect octahedral symmetry, the individual S-F bond dipoles cancel each other out, resulting in a net dipole moment of zero.

Based on this analysis, the molecule with a non-zero dipole moment is SF4 (Sulfur tetrafluoride) due to its asymmetrical geometry caused by the presence of a lone pair of electrons on the sulfur atom.
